endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Document whether your inventory covers only clinical AI or also operational/administrative AI—many organizations start broad and refine scope over time.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: This documentation may include an overview of the AI solution (i.e., who is developing it, date, version, type, citation details, license, etc.), a description of its intended use, and its level of autonomy in decisionmaking.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: The AI system to be deployed is demonstrated to be safe, its residual negative risk does not exceed the risk tolerance, and it can fail safely, particularly if made to operate beyond its knowledge limits.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether recording minimum inventory fields improves governance or patient outcomes, and no study documents how often incomplete records cause harm. The recommendation rests on three frameworks, and only one of them names specific fields such as version and intended use.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support comes from framework statements, which record expert agreement rather than measured effect. A GRADE assessment would treat this as an evidence gap rather than as low-certainty support.

The three sources differ in strength and fit. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide lists developer, date, version, intended use, and autonomy level at a "may" level. The CHAI playbook asks organizations to document inventory scope at a "must" level. The NIST AI 600-1 excerpt addresses safe deployment and risk tolerance but does not name inventory fields.

No supplied study links missing inventory fields, such as an absent monitoring owner or an unrecorded version, to delayed error detection or patient harm. The hazard is plausible, but its frequency and severity have not been measured in the material provided.

commentary.research_gap: Studies could compare health systems with and without required inventory fields. They could measure how often the owner and deployed version of a system can be identified, how long it takes to find affected systems after a vendor update or safety signal, and whether the field burden affects how complete and current the inventory remains.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to maintain inventory records, and the frameworks offer no data on whether minimum-field requirements are feasible in those settings.
